opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When we think about enterprises adopting AI, I usually break the problem into three layers.

The first is the infrastructure layer: compute. GPUs are expensive and scarce, and they behave very differently from the CPUs most IT teams are used to managing. A lot of companies get GPUs, through a cloud provider or a neocloud, and then find that keeping them healthy, scheduled well, and fully utilized is hard. Machines fail, networking is tricky, and utilization is often much lower than people expect. So the first thing we try to solve is making the compute itself reliable and efficient.

The second layer is the software and platform layer between the hardware and the application. Training, fine-tuning, and especially inference all need a stack that's tuned for performance: model serving, batching, quantization, autoscaling, monitoring. This is where my background from Caffe and the frameworks world comes in. The open-source ecosystem is fantastic, but there's still a big gap between "I downloaded a model and it runs on my laptop" and "this serves millions of requests a day with predictable latency and cost." Enterprises don't want to hire a whole team of systems engineers just to close that gap.

The third layer is the application itself, which is where the business value lives. Here we've learned that our job isn't to build the application for the enterprise. It's to make iteration fast and cheap, so that a product team can try a model, measure it, swap it, and ship it without fighting infrastructure every step.

If I had to sum it up, the core problem is efficiency in three senses: cost efficiency, so the economics actually work; engineering efficiency, so small teams can move fast; and operational efficiency, so things don't break at 2 a.m. AI has moved from a research problem to an engineering problem, and much of what enterprises need now is good, solid systems engineering. It's less glamorous than the models themselves, but in my experience that's what decides whether AI actually makes it into production.

r001.rationale: The response describes GPUs as expensive and scarce, with low utilization, and says the goal is to make compute reliable and efficient. This frames cost as getting more out of limited infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It describes a platform that bridges the gap between running a downloaded model and serving it reliably at enterprise scale, so product teams can iterate without fighting infrastructure or hiring a team of systems engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it starts from a pretty simple observation: in enterprise AI, the hard part was never getting a model to produce a nice demo. The hard part is everything between the demo and something that actually runs in production, reliably, at a cost that makes sense.

So when I look at what we need to solve, I break it into roughly three layers.

The first is the infrastructure layer. Enterprises want to use these models, but running them well is genuinely difficult. You have GPU scarcity, you have latency requirements, you have cost pressure, and the models themselves change every few months. Most companies don't want to build an ML systems team just to serve a model. They want it to feel like a cloud primitive, something you call, and it just works, scales, and you pay for what you use. A lot of my background, from Caffe to the work at Facebook and Alibaba, was really about making compute efficient, and that problem hasn't gone away. It's actually gotten bigger with the size of these models.

The second layer is choice and flexibility. Enterprises are rightly nervous about being locked into a single model provider. Open models have gotten very good, and for many workloads they're more than sufficient and much cheaper. But the moment you want to switch, or fine-tune, or run something on your own data under your own compliance rules, you discover the tooling is fragmented. So part of our job is to make the model layer swappable, so a company can pick the right model for each task rather than the one model they happened to sign a contract with.

The third layer, and honestly the one that determines whether any of this matters, is the application gap. Enterprises don't buy tokens, they buy outcomes. They need to connect the model to their data, their workflows, their permissions, and their evaluation criteria. Right now a lot of that is bespoke engineering, done over and over again at every company. I think the real win is making that repeatable, so a team can go from idea to a deployed, monitored AI application in days instead of quarters.

Underneath all of this is a philosophy I hold pretty strongly, which is that the winning platform will be the boring one. Boring in the sense that it's dependable, cost-transparent, and gets out of the way. The excitement should live in what customers build on top, not in the plumbing. My job is to make the plumbing so good that nobody has to think about it.

r001.rationale: It identifies GPU scarcity and cost pressure, then describes efficient compute as an ongoing problem. This frames enterprise AI cost around using limited computing resources efficiently.

r002.rationale: It says companies should not need an ML systems team and models should work like a cloud primitive that users call, with scaling and pay-as-you-go service.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is the business problem, rather than the model. An enterprise usually doesn’t come to you and say, “I need a particular neural network architecture.” They say, “I want to answer customer questions more efficiently,” or “I want to help my employees find information.” Our job is to connect what AI can do with that concrete need.

There are several pieces to that. First, you need to make it easy to build something useful with the company’s own data. Then you need to make it work reliably in production, with the right security, performance, and cost. A demo can be very impressive, but if it takes too long to respond, gives inconsistent answers, or costs more than the value it creates, the enterprise can’t really use it.

So I think a lot of the opportunity is in reducing that complexity. We want developers to spend less time managing infrastructure and more time building the application that makes a difference to their business. And we need to give them flexibility, because models and hardware will keep changing. Adopting a better model should be an improvement they can make, rather than a reason to rebuild everything.

r001.rationale: The response mentions cost and performance, but does not frame cost as getting more useful work from limited computing infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It discusses reducing infrastructure work for developers, but does not say models should be as easy for engineers without AI expertise to use as familiar software services.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what problem the enterprise is trying to solve. People don’t necessarily need an AI model; they need a better way to serve customers, find information, or help employees get their work done. So we have to connect the capabilities of AI to a concrete business outcome.

Then there’s the engineering work that makes it usable. How do you connect a model to the company’s own data? How do you make it reliable, protect that data, and integrate it into an existing application? A demo can look impressive, but running something in production means dealing with latency, cost, and failures every day.

Our job is to make that infrastructure easier to use, so a company doesn’t need a large team of AI specialists just to get started. And because models are changing so quickly, we want to give developers the flexibility to choose what works for their application and improve it over time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions production costs, latency, and failures, but does not frame cost as getting more useful work from limited computing infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure should be easier to use without a large team of AI specialists, but does not compare using AI models to using familiar software services.
